subtopic_detail: extrahepatic features redirecting a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia away from the default diagnosis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 7 week old girl referred with jaundice that began on day four of life and has never cleared. Her parents describe her stools as pale and putty coloured and her nappies as stained dark.

She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her weight has fallen from the 50th centile at birth to the 3rd centile. On examination she has deep set eyes, a broad forehead and a pointed chin, and there is an ejection systolic murmur loudest in the left upper chest that radiates through to her back. A slit lamp examination performed by the ophthalmology registrar shows a prominent ring at the edge of the cornea. A chest radiograph taken to assess the murmur shows a vertebral body at the seventh thoracic level split into two halves.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 150, blood pressure 76/44, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Deep set eyes with a broad forehead and pointed chin, grade 3 ejection systolic murmur in the left upper chest radiating to the back, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, spleen not enlarged, posterior embryotoxon on slit lamp examination
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 168 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 110 micromol/L, gamma glutamyl transferase 620 U/L (less than 100), alanine aminotransferase 145 U/L (less than 40), international normalised ratio within normal limits, alpha 1 antitrypsin level within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows a butterfly vertebra at the seventh thoracic level

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Extrahepatic biliary atresia of the perinatal type
options.rationale: This is the diagnosis that must be excluded urgently in any infant with pale stools and conjugated jaundice, and it remains the default until the extrahepatic features are noticed. It does not cause peripheral pulmonary stenosis, posterior embryotoxon, butterfly vertebrae or the facial phenotype, all of which are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Syndromic paucity of the intrahepatic bile ducts
options.rationale: Conjugated jaundice with a markedly raised gamma glutamyl transferase occurring alongside peripheral pulmonary stenosis, posterior embryotoxon, a butterfly vertebra and the characteristic facial appearance identifies a multisystem disorder rather than isolated liver disease. The combination of cardiac, ocular, skeletal and facial features is what distinguishes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency of the PiZZ phenotype
options.rationale: This is a genuine cause of neonatal cholestasis and is part of the standard workup, but the serum level is within normal limits here. It also produces no cardiac, ocular, skeletal or facial abnormality. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

The inherited canalicular transport defects of types 1 and 2 present with severe cholestasis and intense itch, but characteristically with a gamma glutamyl transferase that is low or within normal limits, which is the opposite of the markedly raised value here. That single enzyme separates them from the other intrahepatic causes. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection of the liver
options.rationale: Congenital infection can produce conjugated jaundice and hepatomegaly and belongs in the differential, but it is typically accompanied by microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and intracranial calcification. It does not produce the cardiac, ocular and vertebral combination described. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced at two weeks of age, or at three weeks if preterm and breastfed, needs a split bilirubin, because a conjugated fraction is never physiological and always requires investigation. The immediate priority is to exclude biliary atresia, since the success of the Kasai portoenterostomy falls sharply after about sixty days of life, and pale stools with dark urine make that the working diagnosis until proven otherwise. Alagille syndrome is the principal alternative and arises from mutations in JAG1 or NOTCH2 affecting the Notch signalling pathway, producing paucity of interlobular bile ducts together with abnormalities in several organ systems. The recognised features are cholestasis, peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot, posterior embryotoxon on slit lamp examination, butterfly vertebrae on a spine or chest film, and a characteristic facies with a broad forehead, deep set eyes and a pointed chin. Distinguishing it from biliary atresia matters because these infants do not benefit from a Kasai procedure and may be harmed by it, and the gamma glutamyl transferase is the enzyme that separates both from the low enzyme familial cholestasis syndromes.
key_points: Any jaundice persisting past two weeks requires a split bilirubin
A conjugated fraction is never physiological and demands urgent assessment
Exclude biliary atresia first because Kasai success falls after about sixty days
Peripheral pulmonary stenosis, posterior embryotoxon and butterfly vertebrae define the syndromic alternative
A low gamma glutamyl transferase points instead to the familial canalicular transport defects
explanation.pearls: A markedly raised gamma glutamyl transferase excludes progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis types 1 and 2, in which the enzyme is characteristically normal or low despite severe cholestasis, making that one enzyme the fastest way to narrow a neonatal cholestasis differential.

subtopic_detail: exertional collapse with a borderline corrected QT interval and a family history of unexplained sudden death
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 14 year old girl in the emergency department after she collapsed during a 400 metre race at her school athletics carnival. Her teacher witnessed the event and says she was unresponsive for about forty seconds, with a few jerks of her arms toward the end, and that she then sat up and spoke normally within a minute.

She was not incontinent and did not bite her tongue, and she had no confusion or drowsiness afterwards. Two years ago she had a similar episode while diving into a swimming pool at a birthday party, which was put down to the shock of the cold water. Her father died at the age of 33 when his car left the road late at night with no other vehicle involved and no explanation found. She takes no regular medications and no over the counter preparations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and fully orientated, no focal neurological deficit, no murmur, normal heart sounds, peripheral pulses normal and symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), magnesium within normal limits, corrected calcium within normal limits, glucose within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute, corrected QT interval 468 milliseconds by the Bazett formula, no delta wave, no Brugada pattern, normal voltages
data_table.Echocardiogram: Structurally normal heart with normal ventricular wall thickness and normal systolic function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that the corrected QT interval is not diagnostic
options.rationale: It is true that a corrected QT of 468 milliseconds falls below the 480 millisecond threshold that is diagnostic on the electrocardiogram alone, and this is precisely the trap. Diagnosis rests on a weighted score that combines the interval with syncope during exertion and a family history of unexplained sudden death before 30, and a borderline interval with those features reaches a high probability. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography and refer to the paediatric neurologist
options.rationale: Brief myoclonic jerks occur commonly in cerebral hypoperfusion from any cause and do not indicate a seizure, and the absence of tongue biting, incontinence and any postictal phase argues strongly against epilepsy. Pursuing the neurological pathway is the classic route by which these children are misdiagnosed for years. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Refer to a cardiac genetic service for family and genetic evaluation
options.rationale: Two exertional collapses, one on entering water, together with a father who died in an unexplained single vehicle crash before 35 and a borderline corrected QT interval, constitute a high probability inherited arrhythmia syndrome that requires specialist evaluation with genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives. Competitive sport is withheld and beta blockade commenced through that service while the assessment proceeds. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor and review the result in the clinic
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring over a single day is unlikely to capture an event that has occurred twice in two years and a normal recording would provide false reassurance. Exercise testing with recovery phase measurement is more informative in this syndrome, and both belong within a specialist assessment rather than instead of one. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Commence propranolol and arrange general practitioner review in six months
options.rationale: Beta blockade is the correct pharmacological treatment and starting it is not the error, but doing so without specialist evaluation leaves the genotype unknown, the family unscreened, the need for an implantable defibrillator unassessed and the sports restriction unaddressed. Relatives at identical risk remain undiagnosed. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Syncope during exertion is a red flag that separates a cardiac cause from the far commoner reflex faint, which occurs on standing, in heat or after a painful stimulus and is preceded by a warning of nausea, greying vision and sweating. Brief myoclonic jerking occurs in up to two thirds of ordinary faints and is not evidence of epilepsy, so the discriminating features are the absence of a postictal phase, of tongue biting and of incontinence, with rapid complete recovery. The congenital long QT syndromes are diagnosed by the Schwartz weighted score rather than by the interval alone, combining the corrected QT, symptom pattern and family history, so an interval between 450 and 480 milliseconds may still indicate disease when it sits alongside exertional syncope and unexplained premature sudden death in a first degree relative. Trigger specificity helps subtype the condition: exertion and swimming point to LQT1, auditory startle and the postpartum period to LQT2, and events during sleep to LQT3. An unexplained single vehicle crash or drowning in a young relative should be recorded as a possible arrhythmic death, since these are the ways sudden arrhythmic deaths are commonly misclassified, and cascade screening of first degree relatives is part of managing the index case.
key_points: Syncope during exertion or on entering water is a cardiac red flag
Myoclonic jerks occur in ordinary faints and do not establish a seizure
Diagnosis uses a weighted score, not the corrected QT interval alone
A corrected QT of 450 to 480 milliseconds can still be diagnostic with supporting features
Unexplained single vehicle crashes and drownings in young relatives may be arrhythmic deaths
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether any relative died young in a single vehicle crash, a drowning or a cot death, because these are the three ways inherited arrhythmic deaths are routinely misclassified and the answer can move a borderline corrected QT of 460 to 480 milliseconds from equivocal to diagnostic.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: first line pharmacotherapy for cyclical mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase on prospective ratings
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who has kept a daily symptom diary for the past two menstrual cycles at your request. She reports two years of irritability, low mood, tearfulness and a sense of being out of control, together with breast tenderness and bloating.

Her diary shows that the symptoms start about six days before each period, build until bleeding begins, and settle within two to three days of the onset of bleeding. Between the end of one episode and the start of the next she rates herself as entirely well and functioning normally at work. She has twice had to leave work early during the worst days and her partner says the arguments are now affecting their relationship. She takes no regular medication and uses condoms for contraception.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination unremarkable at today's visit which falls in the follicular phase, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, haemoglobin within normal limits, ferritin within normal limits, prospective daily ratings across two cycles confirm a symptom free interval of about two weeks in each cycle

lead_in: What would you first recommend as pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral pyridoxine at high dose with evening primrose oil daily
options.rationale: Pyridoxine has modest evidence for physical premenstrual symptoms at low dose but not for the mood syndrome, and doses above 100 mg daily carry a risk of peripheral sensory neuropathy with prolonged use. Evening primrose oil has not been shown to help. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill with a 24 day active regimen
options.rationale: A drospirenone containing pill with a shortened hormone free interval is an effective second line option and is a reasonable choice for a woman who also wants contraception. It has a lower response rate than the serotonergic option and is not the first recommendation when contraception is not being sought. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Cyclical oral micronised progesterone in the second half of the cycle
options.rationale: Luteal phase progesterone has been studied repeatedly for this indication and performs no better than placebo. In some women it reproduces the very symptoms it is intended to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sertraline taken either continuously or in the luteal phase only
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are the established first line treatment for this condition and are distinctive in that they work within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is what makes luteal phase only dosing a viable regimen. Roughly six in ten women respond. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Low dose lithium carbonate with monitoring of the serum level
options.rationale: The cyclical pattern superficially resembles a rapid cycling mood disorder, which is why a mood stabiliser can seem logical, but her mood returns fully to baseline for two weeks of every cycle and is tied to the menstrual cycle rather than running autonomously. Lithium has no established role here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from ordinary premenstrual symptoms by the severity of the mood disturbance and by demonstrable impairment of work, study or relationships, and it is separated from an underlying mood or anxiety disorder by the presence of a genuinely symptom free interval in the follicular phase. Because retrospective recall is unreliable and over attributes symptoms to the cycle, the diagnosis formally requires prospective daily ratings across at least two cycles, which is both a diagnostic step and a therapeutic one since many women find the pattern itself clarifying. The underlying mechanism is an abnormal central response to normal cyclical fluctuations in ovarian steroids and their neuroactive metabolites rather than any abnormality of hormone levels, which is why measuring hormones is unhelpful. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and their rapid onset in this condition, quite unlike their three to four week latency in depression, permits continuous, luteal phase or symptom onset dosing. Second line options include a drospirenone containing combined oral contraceptive with a shortened hormone free interval, and ovarian suppression is reserved for severe refractory cases.
key_points: A symptom free follicular interval separates this from an underlying mood disorder
Prospective daily ratings over two cycles are required for diagnosis
Hormone levels are normal and measuring them does not help
Serotonergic antidepressants act within days here, allowing luteal phase dosing
Luteal phase progesterone performs no better than placebo
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants relieve premenstrual dysphoric disorder within 24 to 48 hours rather than the three to four weeks required in major depression, which is why dosing restricted to the 14 days before menstruation works and halves total drug exposure.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
